text: June 1893. A young Indian lawyer is sitting in a first-class compartment on a train in South Africa.
He has a valid ticket. A white passenger complains. At Peter Merrittsburg Station, he is thrown off the train.
He spent that night shivering in the station waiting room, deciding whether to go home or to fight.
He stayed, and fought, for more than twenty years. His name was Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi.
When he came home to India in 1915, people would come to call him Mahatma, great soul.
His weapon was Satyagraha, holding on to the truth and resisting without violence.
In 1919, in Amritsar, thousands of people gathered peacefully, in a walled garden called
Jallian wallabag. A British general blocked the exits and ordered his troops to fire into
the crowd. They fired until they ran out of bullets. The official count was 379 dead.
Indian estimates were over a thousand.
After Amritsar, millions of Indians who had trusted the British stopped trusting them.
Then Gandhi chose the most unlikely weapon in history.
Remember that Indian cloth?
Remember Manchester?
Gandhi told Indians to burn foreign cloth and spin their own.
He sat at a spinning wheel, the charka, every day, and wore rough homespun cotton called
khadi.
The spinning wheel went on to the freedom movement's flag.
The cloth that had once made India rich would now help set it free.
In 1930, he picked an even stranger target, salt.
The British taxed it, and Indians were banned from making their own.
So Gandhi walked to the sea.
Mr. Gandhi, what exactly are you doing?
Picking up salt.
That's illegal.
Then arrest me, and the thousands behind me.
I'll need a bigger notebook.
The Salt March covered about 380 kilometers in 24 days, and newspapers around the world
followed every step.
Not everyone believed in nonviolence.
Bhagat Singh took up arms and was hanged at 23.
Subhash Chandra Bose raised an army with Japan's help.
And Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, born into a so-called untouchable caste, fought for India's most
oppressed people.
In the Second World War, about two and a half million Indian soldiers fought for Britain,
the largest volunteer army in history.
Meanwhile, in 1943, a famine in Bengal killed around three million people.
By the end of the war, Britain was broke and exhausted.
It could no longer hold on to India.
Freedom was coming, but it was not coming whole.
